title: The Barbarian Invasions
full_review:
Seventeen years ago French-Canadian filmmaker Denys Arcand explored love, sex and politics among a group of highbrow, hedonistic baby boomers in "The Decline of the American Empire." In "The Barbarian Invasions" (Miramax), Arcand revisits the same circle of friends, reuniting the original cast, who have grayed and grown paunchy in the intervening years.

Set in Quebec, the film focuses on the group's truculent torchbearer, Remy (Remy Girard), an erudite history professor and unrepentant philanderer who is diagnosed with inoperable cancer. At Remy's hospital bedside is his ex-wife, Louise (Dorothee Berryman), who, despite a divorce, has maintained an amiable relationship with him.

Unable to reach their seafaring daughter, Louise calls their son, Sebastien (Stephane Rousseau), a wealthy London investment banker, imploring him to return to Canada. Sebastien, whose rocky relationship with his father has kept him away for years, is hesitant to rekindle old antagonisms, but begrudgingly agrees to come home. No sooner is Sebastien off the plane than the two are fighting.

Still harboring resentment over his father's womanizing, Sebastien sees Remy as intolerably contentious. To the self-professed "sensual socialist," Sebastien is a self-righteous "puritanical capitalist," a portent of the coming "barbarian" invasions. Needled by Louise, Sebastien sets about making Remy's remaining time more comfortable by using his financial resources to upgrade Remy to a private room (a feat that involves greasing the palm of the hospital's Mafia-like union boss), paying off Remy's students to visit him, and even employing an addict (Marie-Josee Croze) to illegally purchase and administer heroin to Remy as a painkiller.

More importantly, he organizes a reunion of Remy's bed-hopping buddies. His hospital room is soon abuzz with lusty laughter as the sex-obsessed assembly reminisces about old times, their bacchanalian banality masking shared fears and tears. As Remy's condition worsens, the party shifts to the setting of the first film, a lakeside cottage, lending symmetry to the sequel and bringing the narrative full circle. Serving as a visual metaphor for lost vitality and the approach of death, the autumnal backdrop sets the emotional stage for cathartic mea culpas between father and son. The film ends on a morally bleak note with Remy electing euthanasia.

Reviving their roles from "Decline" are Louise Portal and Dominique Michel as Diane and Dominique, Remy's disillusioned ex-mistresses. Pierre Curzi returns as Pierre, whose former virulently anti-marriage views have given way to bourgeois domesticity. Also returning is Yves Jacques as Claude, an aging homosexual. Johanne Marie Tremblay plays Sister Constance, a Catholic nurse who tackles Remy's skepticism with humor and invites him to "embrace the mystery" of suffering.

Though the film draws comparisons between the sack of Rome and the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, Arcand uses the term "barbarians" to encompass a broad range of toxic influences which he sees as having an erosive effect on society, among them drugs, the health care bureaucracy and unrestrained capitalism. However, flying in the face of Arcand's assertion that the story is ultimately life-affirming are the film's pervasive nihilism and cynical view of traditional morality in favor of sexual autonomy, compounded by its reprehensible solution to suffering -- murder, the most "barbaric" act of all.

In one scene, the concupiscent comrades sit on the cabin's porch listing the ideologies to which they have subscribed over the years. As the camera pans across their abject faces it becomes apparent that it is a litany of despair, a roll call of the 20th century's attempts to replace divine truth with shoddy human substitutes -- all of which have left them existentially unsatisfied.

Despite its la dolce vita overtones, the barren terrain explored is devoid of any genuine hope. The music has stopped; the party is over. The sullen swingers are left reaping the bitter harvest of their chosen life trajectories -- ruined relationships, loneliness, alienation and finally despair. The compassion displayed is a pagan compassion that confuses murder for mercy. In the words of the Catholic novelist Flannery O'Connor, such modern notions of compassion, divorced from moral truth, "lead to the gas chamber" or as the case may be, to a picturesque lakeside cabin in Quebec. The barbarians have conquered from within.

Subtitles.

Due to a cavalier attitude toward promiscuity and adultery, a condoning depiction of assisted suicide, much sexually explicit language and humor, some rough language and profanity, as well as recurring drug abuse, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
